title: Janmashtami: the girl in the cell
hookLine: the baby girl left in Kamsa's cell rises as the Goddess: the Lord's hidden power, revealed
carry: yogamaya: god hides in plain sight

lines: A BABY CRYING IN THE CELL.
cards: Midnight in King Kamsa's prison. Krishna is born, the guards asleep, the chains loose, and Vasudeva carries the baby through the storm and across the Yamuna to the cowherd village.
In Yashoda's house he leaves his son, picks up her newborn daughter, and carries her back through the rain. By morning he's in his cell again, chains on, as if nothing happened.
The guards wake to the sound of a baby crying. They run to tell the king. And Kamsa comes down the stairs to the prison, for the eighth child.

teach.h: SHE SLIPS OUT OF HIS HANDS.
teach.b: Devaki begs him. It's a girl, she says. How could a little girl harm you?
Let me keep just this one. Kamsa doesn't listen. The Bhagavata Purana says he seizes the baby by the feet and swings her to dash her against a stone.
She slips out of his hands. She rises into the air, and in the sky she's no longer a baby.

teach.h: YOGAMAYA, THE GODDESS, IN THE SKY.
teach.b: She's the Goddess, shining, with eight arms and weapons in every hand: Yogamaya, the power of the Lord's own mystery.
It was her power, the Bhagavata says, that put the guards to sleep, and she had been born as Yashoda's daughter to make the whole rescue possible.
She speaks to Kamsa from the sky: the one who will kill you has already been born, somewhere else. Then she's gone. Now the teaching inside this night.
Yogamaya is God's power to hide, and to work while hidden. Krishna himself later says he isn't revealed to everyone, because he's veiled by his yogamaya. Look at how God arrives here.
Not with thunder. Carried through the rain in a basket, raised as a cowherd's boy, while the Goddess lies in a prison cell disguised as a baby girl nobody wanted.
Many Hindus take this to heart: God often works hidden, through ordinary people and ordinary things, and the one everyone overlooks may be the holiest one in the room.
It's part of why, at midnight, many families rock a little cradle with baby Krishna in it. The Lord of the universe, small enough to hold.

teach.h: YOGAMAYA: GOD HIDES IN PLAIN SIGHT.
teach.b: Yogamaya: God hides in plain sight.

how: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, then celebrate Krishna's birth with songs and by rocking a small cradle with an image of baby Krishna; the next day, especially in Maharashtra, teams form human pyramids to break a high-hung pot of curd, called dahi handi.

o: a fast kept for a mother's sake

games.q: who's who on the night — tap the pairs.
p: gave birth to Krishna in prison
raised Krishna in the cowherd village
the Lord's power to hide, and work hidden

s: she slipped from his hands, rose into the sky as the Goddess, and warned him.
the girl told Kamsa his killer was already born elsewhere
the Bhagavata has her speak from the sky, then vanish.
in this story God arrives with thunder and armies
he's carried out in a basket, and the Goddess hides as a baby girl: yogamaya, God working hidden.

games.q: you're one of Kamsa's guards, looking at the crying baby girl in the cell. what's really there?
o: just a baby. nothing to worry about.
the Goddess herself, hidden as a baby girl.
Krishna, swapped back in the night.
games.why: Yogamaya: the Lord's own power, hidden in the one everyone overlooked. she rises from Kamsa's hands as the Goddess.

practice: If you pray, picture the little cradle at midnight, or rock one if your family keeps it, and say softly, Jai Shri Krishna. Stay a moment with God made small enough to hold.
If you don't pray, think of someone you usually overlook, at home, at school, at work, and wonder, just for a minute, what you haven't seen in them. Sit with that, and wait in the dark.

wordCard.voice: Janmashtami. The birth on the eighth night, and a rescue worked in secret by the Lord's own mystery.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the Lord's own power of mystery, who in the story is born as Yashoda's daughter.

carryVoice: Your line: yogamaya: god hides in plain sight. Even in a baby girl in a prison cell. Ninety-two days, and counting.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.3–10.4 (the swap, the guards asleep by Yogamaya's power, Kamsa and the girl, Yogamaya's warning)
Bhagavad Gita 7.25 (Krishna veiled by his yogamaya, not revealed to all)
Janmashtami midnight observance (the cradle of baby Krishna; dahi handi the next day)
